protections: P1: only the image owner (or an admin) may mutate or delete the image, its metadata and its backend data; visibility (public image, shared member) alone must never authorize a mutation.
P2: an image whose protected flag is set must not be deleted (metadata or backend data) on any route, including the v1 and v2 API servers, the registry API and the DB API.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: The registry/DB layer already enforces ownership: image_destroy calls check_mutate_authorization (glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:215) and _image_update does the same (glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:580), so the delete handler looks guarded.

The v2 controller calls the DB API directly and image_update/image_destroy both run check_mutate_authorization, and _get_image already 404s deleted images (glance/api/v2/images.py:142), so the handler looks hardened; hidden unit tests using FakeDB cannot see the check at all.

glance-registry is an internal service normally reached only through the API server; the v1/v2 handlers already reject protected deletes (glance/api/v1/images.py:817, glance/api/v2/images.py:258) and an owner/admin can clear protected through the update path anyway.

glance.db.simple.api is an in-memory test double (glance/tests/unit/utils.py:54) and the configured default data_api is glance.db.sqlalchemy.api (glance/common/config.py:42), so production never runs this code.

Upload is not image deletion; the filesystem store refuses to overwrite existing data (glance/store/filesystem.py:207) and the following image_update enforces ownership, so the early store write looks harmless.

Unprotecting is explicitly supported: the v2 functional test unprotects a protected image and then deletes it (glance/tests/functional/v2/test_images.py:179), so protected is a deletion brake, not an immutability lock; hardening this would break a legitimate flow.
Tags are a separate sub-resource that carries no binary image data and cannot delete an image; the advisories are about image deletion.
This is the update path, not deletion; the binary data is not removed and the later registry update enforces ownership, so the ACL change looks inconsequential.

masking: T3 only becomes the surviving protected-delete route once the API-server guards exist (glance/api/v1/images.py:817, glance/api/v2/images.py:258); the missing shared-layer (image_destroy) guard is masked by the API-layer guard.

conflicts.what: Reordering the v1/v2 store deletion after the DB update (the minimal fix for T1/T2) means a later store failure leaves the image marked deleted while its data survives; the existing error handling at glance/api/v1/images.py:846 and glance/api/v2/images.py:276 must keep working.

A solver hardening T1/T2 by rejecting every operation on protected images would also block the protected-to-False update that the supported unprotect-then-delete flow depends on (glance/tests/functional/v2/test_images.py:179); the coupled writability of protected must be preserved.

fairness_risks: The v2 functional test expects an owner to unprotect a protected image and then delete it (glance/tests/functional/v2/test_images.py:179-190); a security rule making protected images immutable contradicts a legitimate use.
With owner_is_tenant=False the owner is a user id, not a tenant id (glance/context.py:67); checks must compare against context.owner or use the DB is_image_mutable helper, not context.tenant.
Admins must remain able to delete images they do not own (glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:256; glance/tests/unit/v2/test_images_resource.py:645); a naive owner-only check breaks admin and cleanup flows.

Images with owner=None are mutable only by admins (glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:260); a bare equality check lets a context whose owner is None (anonymous/unauthenticated pipeline, glance/api/middleware/context.py:112) match them.

The default unauthenticated-context pipeline sets is_admin=True for every request (glance/api/middleware/context.py:112-121), so any behavioural test of these protections must run the keystone context middleware or the guard is unenforced by configuration.
A deployment using data_api=glance.db.simple.api is in-memory and non-persistent (glance/common/config.py:42); requiring production-grade authorization there may be judged out of scope.

design.why: T1 and T2 are the two independent delete implementations (v1 API server via registry, v2 API server via the DB API) that must both authorize before touching the store, and each carries a different dismissal (registry/DB check for v1, deleted-image 404 plus the direct DB check for v2). T3 is a how-type far-site trap: the protected guard the earlier fix put in the API servers is absent from the shared image_destroy layer, so the registry route survives, and the strong 'internal service' dismissal is exactly what a deep how-type mechanism hides. T4 is the second data_api implementation with no checks at all, dismissed as a test double. The set covers both advisories' protections, both API versions, both services and both DB backends, and every trap is exercisable through existing controller/DB-API test harnesses; T5/T6/T7/T8 are real but adjacent (upload, protected-writability coupling, tags, update ACL side effect) and weaker fits for a deletion-focused task.

unverified: The advisory texts for GHSA-6rrm-xxvh-7r87 (CVE-2012-4573) and GHSA-vwr9-9f8v-vp5m are not present in the worktree; mapping b to the ownership-deletion route is inferred from the supplied summary 'arbitrary deletion of non-protected images' and from the pinned code state, not read from the advisories.

The contents of the a_fix commits (6ab0992e5472, 90bcdc5a89e3, efd7e75b1f41) cannot be inspected: git objects live outside the readable worktree path, so it is unverified whether A is the protected guards in the delete handlers or the DB-layer mutate check now at glance/db/sqlalchemy/api.py:215.

Whether the upstream b fix added a controller-level ownership check or only moved the DB update before the store deletion; both close the side effect, but only a controller-level check is observable through the FakeDB/registry-stub unit harness.

Whether glance-registry is reachable by untrusted clients in the deployments the advisory covers (the default paste pipeline gives it unauthenticated admin context, but it is normally network-internal).
Whether the simple data_api backend is in scope for a production security fix; it is selectable but in-memory and not the default (glance/common/config.py:42).
The exact CVE behind GHSA-vwr9-9f8v-vp5m (possibly one of the 2012-2013 Glance deletion advisories) could not be confirmed offline.
